subject: Fitting a probabilistic learning task with 4 stimuli

messages.author: a33f287fd0620535
messages.subject: Fitting a probabilistic learning task with 4 stimuli
parts:
Hi! Thank you for the great tool. I’m trying to adapt one of the probabilistic reversal learning functions to analyze a similar task.


In our task, participants in an fMRI scanner undergo 200 trials, divided into 2 blocks (100 each). In each trial, participants are shown one of four sets of two stimuli and are asked to choose the stimulus on the left or the right. The sets are:


A | B

B | A

C | D

D | C


A is rewarded 80% of the time and B 20%; C is rewarded 70% of the time and D 30%. The chances of reward are the same regardless of position (left/right). The configuration remains the same in the second block, but the images we use as stimuli change (e.g. A is a hat in block 1 and a rabbit in block 2). 


Participants in our study are divided into two groups: those with ADHD and healthy controls. I am trying to generate fits for the following parameters: positive learning rate, negative learning rate, and choice sensitivity (inverse temperature) for each group. 


Since the expected value of each stimuli are independent, I wondered if one of the functions that includes blocks could be used, with AB and CD trials treated as separate blocks. I reformatted the data accordingly and the prl_rp_multipleB ran without an error, though Apun values are nearly identical and stuck at what appears to be the lower bound (~0.00137). 


To sum up:

1) Can I/how should I fit a probabilistic learning model to a task that includes 4 stimuli?

2) Might treating the stimuli as separate blocks work?


I would appreciate any thoughts and would be glad to share some additional information.


Thank you,


Joel

messages.author: 47d1400f432367d7
messages.subject: Re: Fitting a probabilistic learning task with 4 stimuli
parts:
Hi Joel,

This is a cool application, and hopefully we can help! I have a few clarifying questions:

1) When you go from (A | B) --> (B | A), you said that the stimuli representing A and B both change as well (i.e. only the reward rate is the same). Do you expect any learning from (A | B) to transfer to (B | A)? If not, then you should be able to run this all in a single model with 4 blocks, which will assume that subjects start each block with no knowledge of the expected value of any stimuli. If you do expect some transfer learning, then this gets a bit more complicated.

2) How are the magnitudes of the outcomes coded? For example, is reward = 1, and punishment/no reward = 0? 

3) What do the traceplots and group-level posteriors look like? It could be a convergence problem, which is often the case when parameters are stuck on the bounds. 

Best,
Nate

Ah I see. In that case, you should be just fine using the design that you described, where A and B are stimuli in one block and C and D are in another.
I originally coded them as 1 for reward and 0 for no reward, but I re-coded no reward to -1 for this function. Is that correct?

Your coding scheme of 1 and -1 is the right way to do it. 


The traceplots are definitely worrisome (particularly the inverse temperature being so variable). A pairs plot might be able to show if this is due to some dependencies between parameters. Have you tried looking at such a plot? (i.e. pairs(my_model$fit, pars = c("mu_Apun", "mu_Arew", "mu_beta"))).

Another thing that comes to mind is that maybe participants are performing very differently across blocks for some reason? It might be useful to try fitting the single block model to just one block, and determining if you can do that for each block separately. 

Nate

messages.author: 47d1400f432367d7
messages.subject: Re: Fitting a probabilistic learning task with 4 stimuli
parts:
Yes there is a pretty clear trade-off between the learning rates and inverse temperature parameters. This does occasionally happen when it is hard to identify the learning rates. 

It could also arise from the scale of the reward values relative to the choice sensitivity parameter bounds (i.e. you may get better convergence if beta could be greater than 10). What happens is that when the learning rates are so small, the difference in value between the choices is also small, so the choice sensitivity parameter can become inflated to compensate. That said, you could test this by trying different coding schemes for the reward and punishment values (e.g., reward = 10, punishment = -10, etc.). The relative differences in parameters should be the same, and this should be able to help you determine if the bounds on beta are causing problems.

Nate
